extraction.name: Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS)
extraction.description: A large-scale multilingual read-speech dataset derived from LibriVox audiobooks, covering English, German, Dutch, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Italian, and Polish. It includes approximately 44.5K hours of English and approximately 6K hours across the other seven languages, with transcriptions, training/development/test partitions, limited-supervision subsets, language-model training data, and pre-built language models.
extraction.creator: Vineel Pratap, Qiantong Xu, Anuroop Sriram, Gabriel Synnaeve, Ronan Collobert; Facebook AI Research
extraction.inLanguage: English, German, Dutch, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Italian, Polish
extraction.citeAs: Vineel Pratap, Qiantong Xu, Anuroop Sriram, Gabriel Synnaeve, and Ronan Collobert. MLS: A Large-Scale Multilingual Dataset for Speech Research. Preprint, December 22, 2020. arXiv:2012.03411v2.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: LibriVox APIs were used to measure available audiobook data. Eight languages were selected based on audiobook hours and availability of corresponding text sources. Audiobooks were downloaded using data-preparation tools from the Libri-Light open-source library. English source texts were automatically extracted with parsers for gutenberg.org, archive.org, ccel.org, and hathitrust.org. For other languages, collection combined HTML parsers, copying text from browsers, and extraction from PDF/EPUB books using pdftotext. Alternative sources were manually searched for books with invalid source links. Additional language-model training texts were collected from Project Gutenberg.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Software Collection, Web API, Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Some audiobook text-source links were invalid or redirected to incorrect pages. All spiegel.de text-source links, accounting for one-third of German audio data, redirected to an invalid page; alternative sources were found for most of these books. Some audiobook text sources were not downloaded. Books with corrupted metadata, including missing titles or information about speakers and authors, were removed.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Read audiobooks from LibriVox, most based on Project Gutenberg texts, and their corresponding source-book texts. English text sources included gutenberg.org, archive.org, ccel.org, and hathitrust.org; alternative German sources included projekt-gutenberg.de and zeno.org. Language-model corpus texts came from Project Gutenberg. The LibriVox and Project Gutenberg source data are described as public domain.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Audio was downsampled from 48 kHz to 16 kHz and segmented into 10–20-second utterances. Numbers in matched book text were replaced with aligned words from acoustic-model pseudo-labels. Heuristics modified rare hyphenated or apostrophe-containing words and double apostrophes. Only the latest version of books sharing an author and title was retained. Speakers were assigned to non-overlapping training, development, and test partitions, with gender and duration balancing in development/test sets and duration caps implemented by sampling recordings. Each book chapter appears in only one partition, although books can span partitions. Limited-supervision subsets comprise 10 hours, 1 hour, and six 10-minute sets, with equal sampled duration per gender.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Audio segmentation used acoustic-model token timestamps to split at the midpoint of the longest silence between 10 and 20 seconds, or at 20 seconds when no silence was detected. Text underwent NFKC normalization, removal of punctuation, superscripts/subscripts, emojis and escape symbols, joining of end-of-line-hyphenated words, and filtering to valid Unicode characters for each language's orthography. Candidate transcripts with word error rate above 40% relative to pseudo-labels were discarded. Books with corrupted metadata and multi-speaker recordings were removed. Language-model texts were normalized similarly and filtered to exclude books whose titles had word-level edit distance below 2 from development/test book titles, or whose overlap with an index of development/test 5-grams exceeded one percent.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Acoustic models generated pseudo-labels through beam-search decoding with a 4-gram language model. Source texts were divided into overlapping 1,250-word documents with a 1,000-word stride. Bigram TF-IDF similarity retrieved matching documents, and Smith-Waterman alignment identified the best matching word subsequence as a candidate transcript. Numbers were replaced with aligned pseudo-label words, and hyphen/apostrophe heuristics were applied. Human transcribers reviewed development and test audio while reading generated transcripts and corrected only clear and obvious errors. Speaker gender labels were generated by an RBF-kernel SVM trained on 1,172 LibriSpeech speakers using time-averaged 40-dimensional log-filterbank features.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Smith-Waterman alignment used a match score of 2 and substitution, insertion, and deletion scores of -1. Candidate transcripts were rejected when WER against pseudo-labels exceeded 40%. Human reviewers were instructed to correct only clear and obvious errors to avoid introducing potential transcription bias. Generated-versus-human-rated transcript WER for development/test sets was: English 4.55/4.54, German 3.6/3.9, Dutch 7.24/8.61, French 3.33/4.45, Spanish 1.93/3.07, Italian 6.8/5.37, Portuguese 12.64/12.07, and Polish 5.67/5.12. The gender classifier achieved 95% accuracy on 146 LibriSpeech development/test speakers; manual checks yielded 96% accuracy on Dutch and 94% on Polish.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Time-Depth Separable convolutional acoustic models with Auto-Segmentation Criterion loss; wav2letter@anywhere for streaming inference and token timestamps; beam-search decoding with 4-gram language models; an English pretrained TDS model with CTC loss; bigram TF-IDF retrieval; Smith-Waterman alignment; an RBF-kernel SVM for speaker gender classification.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Speaker identities and gender labels are used to construct and describe dataset partitions. Gender is represented as male/female in the reported statistics. The dataset includes speakers reading in eight languages: English, German, Dutch, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Italian, and Polish.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors intend the freely available dataset to promote open research in large-scale and multilingual automatic speech recognition and to open new avenues in speech recognition and text-to-speech research.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Development and test speakers were balanced by gender and duration, and high-duration speakers' recordings were capped to reduce speaker imbalance. Limited-supervision subsets sampled equal audio duration per gender. Human transcribers were asked to correct only clear and obvious errors to avoid introducing potential bias through human transcription. English development and test sets were deliberately selected to be harder than LibriSpeech dev-other/test-other partitions.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Language selection depended on available audiobook hours and corresponding source texts. The final dataset contains less audio than the source collection because some text sources were not downloaded, candidate transcripts were rejected, or recordings were filtered during partition preparation. Number replacement is imperfect because pseudo-labels may not correctly transcribe the audio. Gender classification is not perfectly accurate. Generated transcripts differed from human-reviewed development/test transcripts, with error rates varying by language. The Polish language model has approximately 13% out-of-vocabulary words, negatively affecting constrained-lexicon decoding performance. Books can overlap across dataset partitions because different chapters may be read by different speakers, although speakers and individual chapters do not overlap.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, development/validation, and testing of automatic speech recognition systems; large-scale and multilingual ASR research; low-resource and limited-supervision benchmarking using 10-hour, 1-hour, and six 10-minute training subsets; language-model training and evaluation; and text-to-speech research, including extending LibriTTS into a larger multilingual resource. English MLS and LibriSpeech training sets are described as interchangeable and complementary, while their development and test sets are independent.
